sampler: Claude Opus 5.5 (in-session; Anthropic API not reachable from this workspace). Prompted for line-for-line translations under four stances, three samples each.

lines: Four great big angels with trumpets in their mouths
will take their places, one on each corner,
to blow: then with a mighty great voice
they'll start to shout: "Out you come, whoever's turn it is!"
Then up will come a long string
of skeletons out of the earth, on all fours,
to take on the shape of persons again,
like chicks around the mother hen.
And this hen will be God the Blessed,
who will make two parts of them, white and black:
one to go down to the cellar, one up on the roof.
Last of all will come out a jingling swarm
of angels, and, as if they were off to bed,
they'll put out the lights, and good night.
Four hulking angels, trumpets at their lips,
will station themselves, one at every corner,
and blow; then in great booming voices
they'll begin to call: "Next! Out, whose turn it is!"
Then up will file a whole rigmarole
of skeletons from the ground, crawling on hands and knees,
to get back the look of people,
like chicks round a broody hen.
And that hen will be God Almighty, bless Him,
who'll divide them in two, the white and the black:
one lot to the cellar, the other to the roof.
At the very end a bell-harness jangle
of angels will come out, and, as if going to bed,
they'll snuff out the lamps, and that's that.
Four whacking great angels with trumpets in their mouths
will set themselves up, one at each corner of the world,
to sound; and then with an almighty voice
they'll begin to cry: "Out, whoever's called!"
Then there'll rise up a nursery-rhyme procession
of skeletons from the earth, on all fours like sheep,
to take on human form again,
like chicks gathered round the hen.
And this hen shall be God, blessed be He,
who will split them in two, the white and the black:
one part for the cellar, one part for the roof.
Finally a jingling troop
of angels will come out, and, as though off to bed,
they will put out the lights, and good night.
Four mighty angels, trumpets set to blow,
shall take their stand, one at each corner placed,
and sound; then, with a voice that fills the waste,
shall cry: "Come forth, whose turn it is below!"
Then from the earth shall rise a long array
of skeletons, all crawling on their knees,
to put on human shape by slow degrees,
like chicks that round a mother hen will stay.
And God the Blessed shall that brood-hen be,
who'll part them in two flocks, the black, the white:
one for the cellar, one the roof shall see.
Last, out shall come a jingling troop, bell-bright,
of angels who, as if to bed they'd flee,
shall douse the lamps, and so, to all, good night.
Four towering angels, trumpets at the mouth,
shall each one take a corner of the earth
and sound; then, in a voice of thunder's girth,
proclaim: "Arise, you summoned, north and south!"
Then shall ascend a chanting litany
of bones from out the ground, on hands and knees,
to clothe themselves in flesh by slow degrees,
like chicks that gather where the hen may be.
That hen shall be the blessed Lord of Hosts,
who'll sunder them in twain, the white, the black:
one to the vaults below, one to the height.
Then, last, shall come a chiming train of hosts
angelic, who, as men retire to rest,
shall quench the lamps; and all is dark. Amen.
Four strapping angels, trumpets in their gobs,
will each stake out a corner of the square
to blast away; then, bellowing through the air,
they'll bawl: "Out, whose turn is it! On with the job!"
Then up will come a nursery-rhyme parade
of skeletons on all fours from the dirt,
to get their human shape back, bone to shirt,
like chicks round mother hen, all unafraid.
And that old hen will be the Lord, God bless,
who'll split them two ways, white lot and black lot:
the cellar for the one, the roof the rest.
Last, out will tumble, jingling like a cart,
a swarm of angels, who, like folk to bed,
will blow the candles out, and that's your lot.
Fower muckle angels wi their trumpets in their mooths
will tak their stance, ane at ilka corner,
an blaw; syne wi a great big voice
they'll stert tae cry: "Oot, whase turn it is!"
Syne up will come a lang rigmarole
o skeletons frae the yird on hauns an knees,
tae tak back the shape o folk,
like chookies roond the clockin hen.
An this hen will be God, bless Him,
that'll pairt them in twa, the white an the black:
ane tae gang doon the cellar, ane up on the ruif.
At the hinner end a jinglin harness-string
o angels comes oot, an, as if gaun tae their bed,
they'll smoor the lichts, an guid nicht.
Fower great hulkin angels, trumpets tae their gabs,
will set theirsels ane at ilka street-neuk,
tae blaw: syne wi an unco roar
they'll begin tae cry: "Next! Oot ye come!"
Then up will file a hale bairnsang
o banes frae the grund, crawlin on aw fowers,
tae get back the look o bodies,
like chickens roond the mither hen.
An yon hen'll be the blessit Lord,
wha'll sort them in twa, the white an the black:
ane fur the cellar, ane fur the riggin.
Last o aw, a jinglin crood
o angels comes oot, an, like gaun tae bed,
they'll pit the lichts oot, an that's that.
Fower muckle angels, trumpets at their mous,
will staun, ane in ilka corner o the warld,
tae soond; syne wi a michty voice
they'll cry: "Come forrit, you that's cried!"
Syne there'll rise a lang string
o skeletons oot the yird, on hauns an knees,
tae tak on human form again,
like chuckies roond the brod-hen.
An this hen sall be God the Blessit,
that'll divide them, white frae black:
ane tae the laigh cellar, ane tae the heich ruif.
At the last, a jinglin train
o angels'll come oot, an, as gin they were gaun tae bed,
they'll douse the lamps, guid nicht tae ye.
Four bloody great angels with trumpets in their gobs
are gonna stand one on every corner
and blow: then with a right old bellow
they'll start yelling: "Out you come, whose turn is it!"
Then up comes a whole long string
of skeletons out the ground on all fours,
to get their shape back as people,
like chicks round a mother hen.
And that hen'll be God, bless him,
who'll split 'em in two, white and black:
one lot down the cellar, one lot up on the roof.
Last of all out comes a jangling gang
of angels, and, like they're off to bed,
they'll turn the lights off, and goodnight.
Four massive angels, trumpets in their mouths,
will plonk themselves one per street corner
to blast it: then with a voice like a foghorn
they'll shout: "Next! Out, whoever's up!"
Then up comes a nursery-rhyme queue
of skellingtons from the dirt, crawling on their knees,
to get back into human shape,
like chicks round the old hen.
And the hen's God Almighty, bless 'im,
who sorts 'em two ways, white and black:
one lot to the basement, one to the roof.
Last of all out jingles a whole jangle
of angels, and, same as going up to bed,
they'll knock the lights off, and Bob's your uncle.
Four whopping angels with trumpets stuck in their mouths
will take up a corner each
to blow: and then in a dirty great voice
they'll start calling: "Oi! Out, whose go is it!"
Then up comes a long old string
of skeletons out of the earth, on all fours,
to put their people-shapes back on,
like chicks round the broody hen.
And this broody hen'll be God, God bless him,
who'll make two piles of 'em, white and black:
one for down the cellar, one for up the roof.
Last thing, out comes a jingly mob
of angels and, like they're turning in,
they'll put the lights out, and night night.
